analysis.one_liner: Adds nursing home and home care coverage to Medicare and gives tax credits to families caring for elderly relatives.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the three House committees it was referred to, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added long-term care — nursing home care and home-based services like aide visits, personal care, and therapy — to Medicare for people who cannot perform at least two daily activities without help, such as bathing, dressing, or eating. It also would have covered up to 80 hours of in-home care per year for chronically dependent people who have a live-in unpaid caregiver, and created a $1,000 income tax credit ($5,000 for a severely impaired dependent) for families supporting an elderly relative in their home. It reauthorized Older Americans Act services with a sliding fee scale based on income. Medicare, then and now, generally does not pay for long-term custodial care, so families pay out of pocket or spend down their savings to qualify for Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Elderly people who need help with daily living, and the working-age adult children who care for them or pay for their care. Medicare long-term care benefits would spare families from draining savings on nursing homes and aides; the tax credit would recognize unpaid family caregiving; and modest sliding-fee protections would shield the poorest seniors from being charged for Older Americans Act services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Elderly needing care and their family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would pay for long-term care services — extended nursing facility care and home-based services including nursing care, aide and homemaker services, personal care, therapies, and caregiver training — for anyone entitled to Medicare who cannot perform at least two activities of daily living without substantial assistance [S3].

Medicare Part B would cover up to 80 hours of in-home care per calendar year for a chronically dependent person who relies on an unpaid live-in caregiver, with any day of 3 hours or less counted as 3 hours so short visits don't erode the limit [S3].

Families maintaining a household with a qualified elderly dependent would get a $1,000 nonrefundable tax credit per dependent, rising to $5,000 if the dependent is severely impaired (unable to perform three or more daily activities), with the credit phased down for adjusted gross incomes above $150,000 [S3].

Older Americans Act services would use a sliding fee scale based on recipients' resources that exempts people with the greatest economic need, and contributions could not be solicited from those recipients [S3].

State case management agencies — generally area agencies on aging, barred from having financial ties to care providers — would assess need, build individual care plans, and run an appeals process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program (and its taxpayers and beneficiaries) would absorb the cost of long-term care benefits, though the bill deliberately punted: it required the agency that runs Medicare to report back by March 1993 with recommendations for financing the benefit through premiums, deductibles, and sliding-scale coinsurance [S3]. Higher-income families (over $150,000 adjusted gross income) would lose the tax credit, and nursing homes and home health agencies would collect Medicare payments while patients pay rising coinsurance — starting at 20% of the cost of extended care in the first six months, rising to 25%, then climbing 10 percentage points each following year [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill created a new Medicare entitlement without funding it: payments would start January 1, 1992, but Congress only required a financing recommendation by March 1993, leaving the program's cost and how to pay for it unresolved [S3].

Patient cost-sharing would grow steeply over time — 20% coinsurance on extended care in the first six months of a care plan, 25% in the next two years, then a 10-point increase each additional year — so the benefit would shrink the longer someone needed care [S3].

The tax credit is nonrefundable, so it helps only families with income tax liability, and the bill caps payment at the amount the case manager recommends, meaning care beyond the plan's hours would come out of the family's pocket [S3].
Support was thin: the bill had 8 cosponsors (6 Republicans, 2 Democrats) and no committee took it up, so it never demonstrated broad backing in Congress [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targeted is real and expensive: Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care, so families either pay tens of thousands of dollars a year or impoverish themselves to reach Medicaid. The home-care, caregiver-training, and tax-credit provisions were sensibly aimed at keeping people in their homes. But the bill was drafted as an aspiration rather than a finished law — it deferred the central question of how to pay for the benefit, and its coinsurance schedule penalized the longest, most expensive cases. As written, Congress would have had to come back and do the hard financing work anyway. It never got that far: no committee gave it a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, then passed to subcommittees within a month, and none of them ever scheduled a hearing or markup, so it quietly expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. William Goodling (R-PA) introduced the bill on April 10, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor committees [S5].
Within weeks it was sent to subcommittees — Health and the Environment (April 22), Health (April 16), and Human Resources (May 10) — and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill had 8 cosponsors, 6 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].
No roll-call vote was ever taken on the bill in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families continued to bear long-term care costs out of pocket or by spending down assets to qualify for Medicaid, and nursing homes kept collecting private-pay and Medicaid rates without a new Medicare payer entering the market. No committee had to make the hard choices about financing the benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Families paying for care; status quo continued

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to reveal a partisan split; the sponsor and 6 of 8 cosponsors were Republicans, but three Democratic-controlled committees never acted, so the bill's death cannot be attributed to a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and home health agencies
industries.note: The bill would have made Medicare a new payer for nursing home and home-based care, routing billions in new revenue to these providers. Ordinary families would gain coverage from the same expansion, so the industry's interest and the public's ran together here, though providers would have faced Medicare payment rules and coinsurance collections.
A Medicare long-term care benefit would reduce demand for private policies sold to cover exactly this gap. Families would be spared premiums, but the private market's role would shrink.

industries.industry: Area agencies on aging (nonprofit case managers)
industries.note: The bill designated area agencies on aging as the permanent gatekeepers who assess need and approve each person's care plan, and barred agencies with financial ties to providers from that role. It locked their central role into the Medicare program while imposing new duties on them.
